article_title: Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring
citation: Olga Manakina, Igor Bogdanov. (2026). Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23814v1
title: IELTS Writing Scored Essays Dataset (Task 2 subset) with released bandit AES implementation
description: The study uses the IELTS Writing Scored Essays Dataset, a publicly available Kaggle resource comprising "787 Academic Task 2 compositions, each accompanied by an official band score ranging from 1 to 9, assigned by qualified IELTS examiners". The compositions respond to conventional Task 2 instructions requiring argument development or perspective presentation. The authors also release their complete implementation code publicly on GitHub and plan to release policy logs.
requirements: Human-assigned official band scores for evaluating agreement between predicted and examiner scores
constraints: The study used only the Task 2 subset; Task 1 essays were excluded from this analysis
target_learners: IELTS test candidates writing Academic Task 2 essays
target_learning_goals: Automated assessment of writing against the official IELTS band-score criteria
examples: Experiments were performed on the Task 2 essay subset with human-assigned scores, employing concurrent processing to maximize throughput.
key_sources: Olga Manakina, Igor Bogdanov. (2026). Learning to Grade Efficiently: A Bandit-Driven Prompt-Selection Framework for Low-Cost LLM Essay Scoring. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23814

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Intersectional Ecological Belonging Model (IEBM)
description: The IEBM is a framework combining intersectionality theory and ecological systems theory to explain how belonging in higher education is shaped by both identity and structure. The article states it 'draws on foundational insights from intersectionality theory (Crenshaw, 1989, 1991; Collins, 1990; Comabehee River Collective, 1982) and ecological systems theory (Bronfenbrenner, 1977, 1995) to explain how students' experiences of belonging in higher education are shaped by both identity and structure.' It maps nested levels—individual, microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem, chronosystem—with intersectionality embedded across all levels rather than treated as a separate layer.
requirements: Analysis must attend to proximal and distal factors, including institutional and structural conditions often neglected in belonging research
constraints: The article presents it as a conceptual framework for research, policy, and practice, not a tested intervention
target_learners: higher education students, especially racially minoritized, first-generation, LGBTQ+, and disabled students
target_learning_goals: understanding and fostering students' sense of belonging in higher education
examples: The model is illustrated with Table 3 scenarios showing how a Black first-gen woman in STEM, an Indigenous student at a land-grant university, and a queer commuter student experience belonging across ecological levels
key_sources: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5

article_title: Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice
citation: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5
title: Six core assumptions of the IEBM
description: The article enumerates six starting-point assumptions for understanding belonging: it is personal and political; structured by multi-level systems; not assimilation ('Students may appear to belong when they conform to dominant norms, but this is a false belonging, premised on erasure of difference'); a shared responsibility with institutions bearing the primary burden; requiring intersectional analysis; and involving agency as well as structure. These assumptions frame how the ecological levels are interpreted and emphasize that institutions, not students alone, are responsible for creating belonging conditions.
requirements: Researchers and practitioners should treat these as starting points rather than fixed truths
constraints: The article notes these are 'not prescriptions or fixed truths but rather starting points'
target_learners: higher education students, particularly marginalized student populations
target_learning_goals: equity-minded understanding of how belonging is produced and constrained
examples: The assumptions are presented as a numbered list preceding the model's visual overview in Fig. 1
key_sources: Royel M. Johnson. (2026). Reframing Belonging in Higher Education: an Intersectional Ecological Model for Research, Policy, and Practice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10104-5

article_title: The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: Beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: Internal/external frame-of-reference (I/E) model of academic self-concept formation
description: The I/E model explains why verbal and math self-concepts are nearly uncorrelated even though verbal and math achievements are substantially correlated: self-concepts form relative to an external social comparison with other students and an internal dimensional comparison across one's own domains. Its 'key theoretical prediction is that the cross-paths leading from achievement in one domain to ASCs in a different (non-matching) domain (e.g., verbal achievement to math self-concept) are negative'. The article cites meta-analytic support (r = .10 for math-verbal self-concepts; cross-path β = −.27) and tests whether the model extends to other self-belief constructs.
requirements: Measures of achievement in at least two school subjects plus domain-specific self-belief measures, analyzed with path models
constraints: The model as originally developed concerns self-concept measures; the article predicts it does not apply to pure self-efficacy items
target_learning_goals: formation of academic self-concept across school subjects
examples: Meta-analytic path analysis cited in the article: math achievement to math self-concept β = .61; verbal achievement to math self-concept β = −.27
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281

article_title: The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system
citation: AlNajdi, S.M. (2022). The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 1105–1124. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10100-4
title: iEN national education portal with books, revisions, and additional resources sub-portals
description: The iEN portal is Saudi Arabia's national education portal, built by the Ministry of Education to integrate technology into the educational system. From its home page "users can log in and access all the benefits in the portal, it has three sub-portals: books and lessons, iEN revisions, and additional resources". It offers AR experiments, e-textbooks, learning games, video clips, and TV channels, and offers role-based accounts for students, teachers, principals, and parents.
requirements: Users sign up to create an account and log in at one of four levels: students, teachers, principals, and parents
target_learning_goals: access to e-learning content, AR experiments, e-textbooks, and revision materials
examples: Appendix A shows the iEN home page with its three sub-portals; Appendices C-F show the four account levels and their services
key_sources: AlNajdi, S.M. (2022). The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 1105–1124. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10100-4

article_title: The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system
citation: AlNajdi, S.M. (2022). The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 1105–1124. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10100-4
title: iEN AR experiments converting textbook experiment pictures into augmented reality
description: The iEN portal provides AR experiments that let students use smart devices to view augmented-reality versions of experiments printed in their textbooks. Per the article, students "could use their smart devices to transfer more than 100 experiments pictures provided in their textbooks to AR experiments". This is the AR capability the study situates QR codes within, linking printed textbook content to virtual content.
requirements: Students need smart devices to scan and view the AR experiments
target_learning_goals: science learning through augmented reality experiments
examples: Appendix B screenshots the AR experiments available on the iEN portal
key_sources: AlNajdi, S.M. (2022). The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 1105–1124. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10100-4

citation: AlNajdi, S.M. (2022). The effectiveness of using augmented reality (AR) to enhance student performance: using quick response (QR) codes in student textbooks in the Saudi education system. Education Tech Research Dev, 70, 1105–1124. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10100-4
title: iEN lesson pages combining video clips, avatar explanations, knowledge maps, and e-books
description: Lesson pages on the iEN portal package several asynchronous learning resources for each lesson. As the article describes, the page "provides clips to explain experiments, other clips explained the lesson in an avatar video, video clips provided asynchronous teaching, a clip summarizing the lesson in a knowledge map, and an e-book". These pages supported remote teaching during the COVID-19 transition and accompany the textbook units studied.
requirements: Access requires an iEN account and internet connectivity
target_learning_goals: understanding lesson content through video, avatar, knowledge-map, and e-book formats
examples: Appendix H screenshots one lesson page showing the clip, avatar video, knowledge map, and e-book components

article_title: Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners' Writing Ability: Teachers' Practices and Beliefs
citation: Hosseini, H., Chalak, A., & Biria, R. (2019). Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners’ Writing Ability: Teachers’ Practices and Beliefs. International Journal of Instruction, 12(2), 33-50. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.1223a
title: IELTS Writing Task 1 pre-test/post-test assessment with four band-descriptor criteria
description: The study used two versions of IELTS Writing Task 1 as pre-test and post-test, scored by two examiners on the four IELTS writing marking criteria: "task achievement, cohesion and coherence, lexical resource (vocabulary) and grammatical range and accuracy", each worth 25% of the total marks. The same task type was used at both time points to measure improvement, and the structure mirrored a formal IELTS writing exam. This instrument served as the dependent-variable measure for both groups.
requirements: Two examiners (raters) assessed writings on the four marking criteria
constraints: The article notes generalization of results "should be done more cautiously" regarding external validity
target_learners: Iranian intermediate EFL learners preparing for IELTS
examples: One version of IELTS Writing Task 1 was used as the pre-test and another version as the post-test
key_sources: Hosseini, H., Chalak, A., & Biria, R. (2019). Impact of Backward Design on Improving Iranian Advanced Learners’ Writing Ability: Teachers’ Practices and Beliefs. International Journal of Instruction, 12(2), 33-50. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2019.1223a

article_title: The effects of early childhood mental health consultation on early childhood teachers' perceptions of children's challenging behaviors, expulsion risk, and the moderating role of teaching stress.
citation: Trigg, A. B., Keyes, A. W., Gray, S., Hatch, V., Brunet, K. T., & Heller, S. S. (2026). The Effects of Early Childhood Mental Health Consultation on Early Childhood Teachers' Perceptions of Children's Challenging Behaviors, Expulsion Risk, and the Moderating Role of Teaching Stress. Infant Mental Health Journal, 47, e70079. https://doi.org/10.1002/imhj.70079
title: IECMHC theory of change (Center of Excellence framework)
description: The TIKES program follows the IECMHC theory of change from the Center of Excellence for Infant and Early Childhood Mental Health Consultation. The article states the framework "posits the direct effects of an IECMHC program are realized by increasing consultees' capacity to promote infant and early childhood mental health," with indirect effects including program adjustments, reductions in disparities, and positive child and family impacts. Consultee and consultant characteristics (education, race, experience) shape engagement in consultation, which in turn shapes direct outcomes (consultee capacity) and indirect outcomes such as reduced child mental health problems and reduced expulsion.
requirements: Engagement in the consultation relationship (relationship development, readiness for consultation) as the pathway linking consultant and consultee characteristics to outcomes
constraints: The framework distinguishes direct effects (consultee capacity) from indirect effects; the present study examined teacher-perception outcomes as potential short-term direct impacts, not actual expulsions
target_learners: Early childhood teachers, families, programs, and systems serving children from birth to age six
target_learning_goals: Increasing consultees' capacity to prevent, identify, treat, and reduce the impact of mental health problems among young children
examples: Prior research on this program reported improved CLASS-PK Emotional Support and Classroom Organization and higher teaching self-efficacy after consultation, with gains maintained six months later

The Effects of Early Childhood Mental Health Consultation on Early Childhood Teachers' Perceptions of Children's Challenging Behaviors, Expulsion Risk, and the Moderating Role of Teaching Stress.
